government.note: Federal parliamentary constitutional monarchy and Commonwealth realm. The monarch of the United Kingdom is also King or Queen of Canada and is represented by the Governor General, appointed on the Prime Minister's advice. The Prime Minister depends on the confidence of the elected House of Commons; the Senate is appointed. No national referendum has been held since 1992.

offices.note: The Canadian Crown is held by the same person as the British Crown (Elizabeth II until 2022, then Charles III). Represented in Canada by the Governor General.

system.note: Single-member ridings by first past the post: 301 seats in 2000, 308 from 2004, 338 from 2015, 343 from 2025. Maximum term five years; fixed election dates (four years) since 2007, but early elections remain possible. seats_2000 is the 1997 result (Lib 155, Ref 60, BQ 44, NDP 21, PC 20, Ind 1) adjusted for changes the Wikipedia member list dates to 1998-1999: Sherbrooke by-election 1998 (PC to BQ), Port Moody-Coquitlam by-election 1998 (Reform to Liberal), Bill Matthews (PC to Liberal, 1999), Angela Vautour (NDP to PC, 1999), Rejean Lefebvre (BQ to independent, 1999) and Jake Hoeppner (Reform to independent, 1999). These adjusted figures reconcile exactly with the standings at dissolution in October 2000 after the 2000 floor crossings. The Speaker (Gilbert Parent) is counted with the Liberals.

system.note: Senators are appointed by the Governor General on the Prime Minister's advice and serve until age 75. seats_2000 uses the standings on election day 1997 (Liberal 51, PC 50, independents 3, 104 senators then) because no 1 January 2000 figure was found; one seat is entered as vacant to reach 105. By dissolution in October 2000 the Liberals held 56 and the PCs 35.
